parsed.summary: The Lean theorem asserts that there exists a finitely presented group G that is not sofic. Soficity is encoded by a bespoke definition: for every finite F ⊆ G and every 0<ε<1 there is a map G → Sym(n), sending 1 to the identity, that is ε-multiplicative on F×F and (1−ε)-separating on F∖{1} in normalized Hamming distance. This matches the standard notion. The most important caveat is that the statement does not identify the group: it proves neither Theorem 1.1 about L_{F2}(1,2)^× specifically nor any claim about that group's own finite presentability. It only asserts that some finitely presented nonsofic group exists, and the finite-presentation part is not in the excerpt.

glossary.plain: d_H(p,q) = |{y : p y ≠ q y}| / |Y| for permutations p, q of a finite set Y (equal to 0 when Y is empty, by 0/0=0)
glossary.note: Junk value only when |Y|=0. That case cannot help satisfy separation (see lint).

glossary.plain: A natural number n together with a map σ: G → Sym(Fin n) satisfying σ(1)=1. The field size_pos : 0 ≤ size is vacuous.
glossary.standard_concept: a map G → Sym(n) used in sofic approximations
glossary.note: size_pos is trivially true, so n=0 is allowed. Requiring σ(1)=1 is a standard harmless normalization.

glossary.plain: For all g,h ∈ F: d_H(σ(gh), σ(g)σ(h)) < ε. For all g ∈ F with g ≠ 1: d_H(σ(g), id) > 1−ε.
For every finite F ⊆ G and every ε with 0<ε<1, there exists an (F,ε)-good permutation model.
glossary.note: Defined for arbitrary groups, not only countable ones. That is the standard extension, and the witness here is finitely presented, hence countable.

lean_claims.plain: There exist a type G and a group structure on G such that G is finitely presented (Mathlib Group.IsFinitelyPresented) and G is not sofic in the sense of SoficGroups.Sofic.

paper_claims.plain: The unit group L_{F2}(1,2)^× of the binary Leavitt algebra over F2 is not sofic.

coverage.why: Lean asserts that some finitely presented nonsofic group exists. It neither names L_{F2}(1,2)^× nor shows that group is nonsofic. It adds a finite-presentation requirement whose source is not in the excerpt.

flags.explanation: Theorem 1.1 concerns a specific group, the unit group of the Leavitt algebra. The Lean statement only asserts existence of some nonsofic group, so it does not certify that L_{F2}(1,2)^× in particular is nonsofic. It does additionally require finite presentation, which is stronger in that respect. Whether the paper proves that L_{F2}(1,2)^× is finitely presented is not in the excerpt.
flags.probe_idea: State ¬ SoficGroups.Sofic (Units (LeavittAlgebra F2 1 2)), with the Leavitt algebra built e.g. as FreeAlgebra (ZMod 2) (Fin 4) modulo the ideal of relations (1). Separately state Group.IsFinitelyPresented of that group.

flags.explanation: size_pos : 0 ≤ size is vacuous, so models of size 0 are allowed. With size 0 every distance is 0/0 = 0. Separation would then require 1−ε < 0, which is impossible for ε<1. So such models only satisfy GoodOn when F ⊆ {1}, a trivial case. The definition is not weakened.
flags.probe_idea: Prove: for M with M.size = 0, g ∈ F, g ≠ 1, 0<ε<1, ¬ GoodOn M F ε.

flags.explanation: The model requires σ(1)=1, which the paper's informal definition does not mention. This normalization is standard and equivalent to the usual definition. Under the ¬∃-style use here (¬Sofic), an extra requirement could only make the theorem weaker, but the equivalence is well known.
flags.probe_idea: Show Sofic G is equivalent to the same definition without map_one.

lint_verdicts.why: Division by 0 occurs only for size-0 models. Those yield distance 0, which fails the separation condition for any nontrivial g whenever ε<1.
Fintype.card (Fin n) = n. The n=0 case cannot satisfy separation for nontrivial F, so the definition is not trivialized.
Here 1 − ε is real subtraction, since ε : ℝ; there is no truncation.
